facts: Rigid lithospheric plates move above mantle rock that remains solid yet can flow slowly, while heat transfer sustains mantle convection.
Upward mantle flow at ocean ridges helps form new lithosphere while plates diverge.
At convergent boundaries, one plate can be subducted into the mantle beneath another.

keyTerms.df: Lithospheric plates are rigid structures that move above slowly flowing solid mantle rock.
keyTerms.eg: At convergent boundaries, one lithospheric plate can be subducted beneath another.
keyTerms.mi: The rigidity of lithospheric plates means they cannot move above mantle rock.
keyTerms.cx: Rigid plates do move over mantle material that flows slowly while remaining solid.

keyTerms.df: Mantle convection is sustained by heat transfer as solid mantle rock flows slowly.
keyTerms.eg: Heat transfer sustains mantle convection beneath moving lithospheric plates.
keyTerms.mi: Mantle convection requires mantle rock to stop being solid.
keyTerms.cx: The moving mantle material retains its solid state as it flows slowly.

keyTerms.df: Ocean ridges are settings where upward mantle flow helps form new lithosphere as plates diverge.
keyTerms.eg: At ocean ridges, new lithosphere forms while plates move apart.
keyTerms.mi: Ocean ridges are convergent boundaries where one plate is subducted beneath another.
keyTerms.cx: These ridges coincide with upward mantle flow and plate divergence.

scenario.su: A mapper must label a boundary represented by upward mantle flow at an ocean ridge and plates diverging. The available labels distinguish ocean-ridge lithosphere formation from convergent-boundary subduction, so the mapper must choose one despite the shared involvement of mantle and plates.
scenario.ma: Students compare the ocean-ridge observation showing upward mantle flow and diverging plates, the convergent-boundary passage describing one plate subducted beneath another.

mc.q: A comparison notes that rigid lithospheric plates move above mantle rock while heat transfer sustains mantle convection; which proposition preserves the distinguishing behavior of the mantle rock?
op: Solid mantle rock can flow slowly
Rigid lithospheric plates can flow slowly
Mantle convection moves above rigid lithospheric plates
Heat transfer sustains rigid lithospheric plates
mc.ex: Mantle rock remains solid yet can flow slowly beneath moving rigid lithospheric plates. Slow flow describes the mantle rock, not the rigid plates.

mc.q: A mapper observes upward mantle flow at an ocean ridge while plates diverge and must choose between lithosphere formation and subduction; which interpretation fits the recorded case?
op: Upward mantle flow helps form new lithosphere
Diverging plates subduct beneath one another
Ocean ridges mark convergent plate motion
New lithosphere causes upward mantle flow
mc.ex: At ocean ridges, upward mantle flow helps form new lithosphere while plates diverge. Subduction instead describes one plate descending beneath another at convergent boundaries.

facts: A natural experiment uses a policy change or external event affecting one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observational data.
The causal claim is credible only if the two groups were comparable apart from the change.
The effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor only when that comparability holds.

keyTerms.df: A natural experiment estimates a causal effect from observational data using a change that affects one group but not another.
keyTerms.eg: A policy change affecting one group but not another is used with observational data to estimate a causal effect.
keyTerms.mi: A natural experiment requires the policy change to affect both groups.
keyTerms.cx: Its defining comparison has the change affect one group but not another.

keyTerms.df: A causal claim is credible when the compared groups were comparable apart from the policy change or external event.
keyTerms.eg: A causal claim is treated as credible when the two groups were comparable apart from the change.
keyTerms.mi: A causal claim makes the two groups comparable apart from the change.
keyTerms.cx: Group comparability supports credibility; it is not produced by making the claim.

keyTerms.df: A confounding factor is distinguished from the policy when group comparability supports attributing the effect to the policy.
keyTerms.eg: When the groups are comparable, the effect is attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor.
keyTerms.mi: A confounding factor receives the policy attribution when group comparability holds.
keyTerms.cx: With comparability, attribution goes to the policy rather than the confounding factor.

scenario.su: An analyst observes a policy change affecting one group but not another and must decide whether the estimated effect can be attributed to the policy. A deadline requires a decision while the comparability of the groups remains disputed.
scenario.ma: policy-change record identifying the affected group, observational-data comparison of the estimated effect, group-comparability assessment covering conditions apart from the change

mc.q: A natural experiment records a policy change affecting one group but not another, while a comparison shows group comparability; what distinction supports the causal claim?
op: Causal effect estimates the natural experiment
Natural experiment estimates; comparability supports causal credibility
Group comparability follows from causal credibility
Causal claim establishes comparability between groups
mc.ex: The unequal exposure identifies the natural-experiment comparison, while group comparability supports the causal claim's credibility. The causal claim does not establish comparability; comparability must support its credibility.

mc.q: A policy affected one group but not another, and records show the groups were comparable apart from the change; what decision about the observed effect is supported?
op: Treat the causal claim as creating comparability
Attribute the effect to the policy
Attribute the policy to a confounding factor
Attribute comparability to the observed effect
mc.ex: Because the records establish group comparability apart from the change, the effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor. The causal claim does not create group comparability.

facts: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

keyTerms.df: A class defines a type of object and serves as its blueprint.
keyTerms.eg: A class is used as the blueprint for creating objects.
keyTerms.mi: A class is an individual object created from a blueprint.
keyTerms.cx: The created individual is an instance; the class supplies the blueprint.

keyTerms.df: Objects are entities built from a class, with each one called an instance.
keyTerms.eg: Objects created from a class are individual instances.
keyTerms.mi: Objects define the methods shared by every instance.
keyTerms.cx: The class defines the shared methods, while objects are built from that class.

keyTerms.df: Instances are individual objects whose attributes are carried as their own copies.
keyTerms.eg: Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes.
keyTerms.mi: Instances define the methods that the class shares.
keyTerms.cx: Methods come from the class and are shared by its instances.

scenario.su: Students must classify a class and two objects as either a blueprint or instances before a deadline. They must also distinguish the separate attribute copies from the methods shared by both objects.
scenario.ma: class passage stating that it is a blueprint for creating objects, object passages identifying two individual objects created from the class, attribute observation showing each instance carrying its own copy, method observation showing class-defined methods shared by both instances

mc.q: When a class is observed defining a type and an object is observed being built from it, which comparison correctly distinguishes the exact terms class and instance?
op: Class is blueprint; built object is instance
Class is instance; built object is blueprint
Instance is blueprint; class is built object
Object is class; blueprint is instance
mc.ex: The class is the blueprint, and an object built from it is an instance. Calling the instance the blueprint reverses the stated relationship.

mc.q: Two objects each carry separate attribute copies but use methods defined by their class; under a complete-comparison constraint, which account fits these observations?
op: Instances copy attributes and share class methods
Instances carry their own attribute copies
Instances share attributes and copy class methods
Class methods are shared by instances
mc.ex: Each instance has its own attribute copy, while the class-defined methods are shared by the instances. Saying attributes are shared and methods copied reverses both relationships.

facts: Synovial joints are common movable joints with a joint cavity, articular cartilage, synovial fluid, and supporting ligaments that allow smooth motion.
A key structural feature of a synovial joint is a fluid-filled joint cavity.
Ligaments support synovial joints by holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion.

keyTerms.df: A joint cavity is a key structural feature of a synovial joint.
keyTerms.eg: The fluid-filled joint cavity is identified in a synovial joint.
keyTerms.mi: The joint cavity holds bones together and resists abnormal motion.
keyTerms.cx: Holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion describes ligaments, not the joint cavity.

keyTerms.df: Ligaments are supporting structures that hold bones together and resist abnormal motion.
keyTerms.eg: Ligaments support a synovial joint during smooth motion.
keyTerms.mi: Ligaments are the fluid-filled cavity of a synovial joint.
keyTerms.cx: The fluid-filled cavity is the joint cavity; ligaments provide support by restraining abnormal motion.

keyTerms.df: Synovial fluid is one component listed for common movable synovial joints.
keyTerms.eg: A synovial joint includes synovial fluid with articular cartilage.
keyTerms.mi: Synovial fluid supports joints by holding bones together.
keyTerms.cx: That supporting relation belongs to ligaments, while synovial fluid is a listed joint component.

scenario.su: A student must classify a common movable joint from a notation describing a fluid-filled joint cavity and supporting ligaments. The decision is constrained to distinguishing the cavity observation from the ligament observation before the deadline.
scenario.ma: fluid-filled joint cavity notation, supporting ligaments observation, common movable joint description

mc.q: A comparison records a fluid-filled joint cavity and ligaments resisting abnormal motion; which distinction correctly assigns these two observed properties to the exact lesson terms?
op: Ligaments are fluid-filled; joint cavity resists abnormal motion
Joint cavity holds bones; ligaments contain synovial fluid
Joint cavity resists abnormal motion; ligaments hold bones
Joint cavity is fluid-filled; ligaments resist abnormal motion
mc.ex: The joint cavity is fluid-filled, while ligaments resist abnormal motion. Assigning resistance to the joint cavity reverses the stated ligament relation.

mc.q: A reviewer must label a joint by the deadline and observes a fluid-filled joint cavity plus ligaments holding bones together; which notation most directly supports a synovial joint classification?
op: Ligaments are the fluid-filled joint cavity
Synovial fluid resists abnormal motion
Joint cavity holds bones together
Fluid-filled joint cavity supports synovial joint label
mc.ex: A fluid-filled joint cavity is a key structural feature of a synovial joint. Holding bones together describes ligaments, not the joint cavity.

facts: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost, even if another producer is better at making everything.
When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.
Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill.

keyTerms.df: Opportunity cost is the distinguishing basis used to identify which producer has comparative advantage in a good.
keyTerms.eg: For a good, the producer with the lower opportunity cost has comparative advantage.
keyTerms.mi: The producer better at making everything must hold the comparative advantage in every good.
keyTerms.cx: Being better at everything does not prevent another producer from holding comparative advantage through a lower opportunity cost.

keyTerms.df: Total output is an outcome that rises when producers specialize according to comparative advantage and then trade.
keyTerms.eg: After each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and trades, total output rises.
keyTerms.mi: Trade makes total output fall after producers specialize according to comparative advantage.
keyTerms.cx: Following comparative-advantage specialization with trade raises production rather than reducing it.

keyTerms.df: Absolute skill is the property of being better at making everything, which differs from having a lower opportunity cost.
keyTerms.eg: Another producer may be better at making everything while a producer still has comparative advantage in a good.
keyTerms.mi: Differences in absolute skill are the source of gains from trade.
keyTerms.cx: Trade gains arise from differences in opportunity cost rather than from who is better at making everything.

scenario.su: A policy analyst must decide whether two producers' records support comparative-advantage specialization and gains from trade. The decision is due before a deadline, while one producer is better at making everything but the opportunity-cost entries favor the other producer for a good.
scenario.ma: opportunity-cost table for each good, specialization notation for each producer, total-output measurements before and after trade, consumption records for trade and production alone

mc.q: Records show one producer has lower opportunity cost for a good while another is better at making everything. Which comparison identifies comparative advantage and distinguishes the source of gains from trade?
op: Absolute skill, not lower opportunity cost
Absolute skill differences produce trade gains
Lower opportunity cost, not absolute skill
Better at everything means comparative advantage
mc.ex: Comparative advantage and gains from trade are grounded in differences in opportunity cost. Being better at making everything does not make absolute skill the source of trade gains.

mc.q: Two producers specialize according to comparative advantage and then trade; records show higher total output and consumption beyond production alone. Which sequence should the analyst record despite the deadline?
op: They specialized by absolute skill, then traded
They specialized by comparative advantage, then traded
They specialized by comparative advantage
They traded, then specialized by comparative advantage
mc.ex: The observed rise in total output and consumption beyond production alone follows specialization according to comparative advantage and then trade. Specialization alone omits the trade required by the supported sequence.

facts: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

keyTerms.df: A class is the blueprint that defines a type of object with attributes and methods.
keyTerms.eg: A class provides the blueprint from which objects are built.
keyTerms.mi: Each class is an individual object created from an instance.
keyTerms.cx: The blueprint is the class, whereas an object created from it is an instance.

keyTerms.df: An instance is an individual object created from a class blueprint.
keyTerms.eg: Two objects built from one class are two instances.
keyTerms.mi: An instance defines the shared methods for every class.
keyTerms.cx: Shared methods are defined by the class; an instance is an object built from that class.

keyTerms.df: Attributes are the data for which each instance carries its own copy.
keyTerms.eg: Two instances carry separate copies of the attributes.
keyTerms.mi: Attributes are shared by every instance like class-defined methods.
keyTerms.cx: Attribute copies belong to individual instances, while the class-defined methods are shared.

scenario.su: Before a deadline, a reviewer must classify a blueprint record and two object records using the labels class and instance. The records show attributes and methods in the blueprint, separate attribute copies in the objects, and shared class-defined methods, but the labels are missing.
scenario.ma: blueprint notation listing attributes and methods, first object record with its attribute copy, second object record with its attribute copy, method notation shared by the object records

mc.q: Two objects show separate attribute records while referring to the same class-defined methods. Which statement correctly distinguishes how attributes and methods relate to these instances?
op: Instances share attributes; class methods are copied
Classes copy attributes; instances share methods
Instances carry attributes and define shared methods
Instances copy attributes; class methods are shared
mc.ex: Each instance carries its own attribute copy, while methods defined by the class are shared by every instance. The reversed view incorrectly makes attributes shared and methods separately copied.

mc.q: A blueprint record creates two individual object records, and a deadline requires assigning the labels class and instances. Which labeling is supported by the observed relationship?
op: Label blueprint object and created objects classes
Label blueprint instance and created objects classes
Label blueprint class and created objects objects
Label blueprint class and created objects instances
mc.ex: A class is the blueprint for creating objects, and the individual objects created from it are instances. Calling the blueprint an instance reverses the supplied relationship between the class and its created objects.

facts: A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.
Unlike a price-taking competitive firm, a monopoly is a price maker: it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells.
Because it produces less and charges more than a competitive market, a monopoly creates deadweight loss.

keyTerms.df: A monopoly is a market distinguished by a single seller, no close substitutes, and barriers to entry.
keyTerms.eg: A market record shows a single seller, a product with no close substitutes, and barriers to entry.
keyTerms.mi: A market becomes a monopoly whenever its seller restricts quantity.
keyTerms.cx: Restricting quantity describes how a price maker can raise price, not the market features required for monopoly classification.

keyTerms.df: A price maker is a monopoly that can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells.
keyTerms.eg: The monopoly restricts the quantity it sells and the recorded price rises.
keyTerms.mi: A price maker must produce more to raise price.
keyTerms.cx: The stated price increase follows a quantity restriction, rather than an expansion of production.

keyTerms.df: Deadweight loss is created when a monopoly produces less and charges more than a competitive market.
keyTerms.eg: The monopoly record shows less production and a higher charge than the competitive market record.
keyTerms.mi: Deadweight loss occurs when a monopoly produces more and charges less than a competitive market.
keyTerms.cx: The relevant comparison runs in the opposite direction: monopoly quantity is lower and its charge is higher.

scenario.su: An analyst must classify a market before a deadline using records showing one seller, no close substitutes, barriers to entry, restricted quantity, and a raised price. The analyst must also decide whether a comparison showing less production and a higher charge than a competitive market supports deadweight loss, despite a notation describing a competitive firm as price-taking.
scenario.ma: seller-count record showing a single seller, substitute observation showing no close substitutes, entry notation showing barriers to entry, quantity-price comparison showing less production and a higher charge than a competitive market

mc.q: A comparison shows that a monopoly restricts quantity and raises price, while a competitive firm is described as price-taking; which distinction matches these observations?
op: Monopoly price maker; competitive firm price-taking
Monopoly price-taking; competitive firm price maker
Both firms price makers through quantity restriction
Both firms price-taking despite quantity restriction
mc.ex: The monopoly can raise price by restricting quantity, whereas the competitive firm is price-taking. Reversing those roles contradicts the stated comparison.

mc.q: Records show one seller, no close substitutes, entry barriers, less production, and a higher charge than a competitive market; which case assessment is supported before the deadline?
op: Monopoly conditions with deadweight loss
Competitive market conditions with deadweight loss
Monopoly conditions with greater production
Monopoly conditions with a lower charge
mc.ex: One seller, no close substitutes, and entry barriers identify monopoly conditions, while less production and a higher charge support deadweight loss. Competitive market conditions do not fit the recorded market features.

facts: A user scenario is a narrative that situates a user type, motivation, context, goal, and tasks in a specific interaction.
Scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction for a specific user.
A scenario should state who the user is, why and where they act, what goal they have, and how they pursue it.
Scenario work can reveal how needs vary with context and across diverse users.
Teams should validate and refine scenarios with the represented user group and collaborators.

keyTerms.df: A user scenario is a narrative distinguished by situating specified user elements within a specific interaction.
keyTerms.eg: A team writes who the user is, why and where they act, their goal, and how they pursue it.
keyTerms.mi: A user scenario communicates a design idea without situating a user type or context.
keyTerms.cx: The narrative must place the user type and context within the interaction, so those elements cannot be omitted.

keyTerms.df: A specific interaction is the setting through which scenarios communicate a design idea for a specific user.
keyTerms.eg: A scenario connects a specific user, goal, and tasks within the interaction.
keyTerms.mi: A specific interaction replaces the need to identify who acts and what goal they have.
keyTerms.cx: The interaction does not replace those details; the scenario should state the user and goal as well.

keyTerms.df: The represented user group is a participant in the validation and refinement of scenarios alongside collaborators.
keyTerms.eg: Teams ask the represented user group and collaborators to validate and refine a scenario.
keyTerms.mi: Collaborators should refine scenarios before the represented user group validates them separately.
keyTerms.cx: Both the represented users and collaborators belong in validation and refinement, rather than being assigned separate roles.

scenario.su: Before a deadline, a team must choose which scenario draft is defensible: one states the user, context, goal, and tasks, while the other states a design idea and specific interaction. The team must classify each draft using its recorded contents despite pressure to select one immediately.
scenario.ma: draft notation listing user, context, goal, and tasks, draft passage stating a design idea through a specific interaction for a specific user

mc.q: A reviewer compares a narrative that situates user elements with scenarios that present a design idea; which distinction correctly describes the narrative and the specific interaction?
op: Narratives communicate contexts; scenarios situate specific users
Narratives situate elements; scenarios communicate design ideas
Narratives situate design ideas; scenarios communicate user types
Narratives communicate users; scenarios situate design ideas
mc.ex: A user-scenario narrative situates the user elements, while scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction. Assigning the design idea to what the narrative situates swaps these relationships.

mc.q: A team compares scenario drafts before review: one records who, why, where, the goal, and its pursuit, while the others omit a recorded element. Which draft should it select?
op: Choose why, where, goal, and pursuit
Choose who, why, where, goal, and pursuit
Choose who, where, goal, and pursuit
Choose who, why, where, and goal
mc.ex: A scenario should state who acts, why and where they act, their goal, and how they pursue it. Stopping at the goal omits how the user pursues it.

facts: A research-based persona is a shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence.
Personas are one way to present research findings so other people can understand and share them.
User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.
Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs.
Keeping each user story linked to its source need enables evaluation of whether the need is being met.

keyTerms.df: A research-based persona is a shareable profile representing a user group with similar behavior and needs.
keyTerms.eg: A team shares a research-based persona that profiles a user group with similar behavior and needs.
keyTerms.mi: A research-based persona describes features and content intended to meet user needs.
keyTerms.cx: Features and content belong in user stories, whereas the persona profiles a user group.

keyTerms.df: User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.
keyTerms.eg: A team turns user needs into user stories intended to meet those needs.
keyTerms.mi: User needs describe features and content intended to meet user stories.
keyTerms.cx: Teams instead turn needs into stories, and the stories carry the feature and content descriptions.

keyTerms.df: User stories can remain linked to source needs so whether those needs are met can be evaluated.
keyTerms.eg: A user story describes features and content intended to meet its source need.
keyTerms.mi: User stories are shareable profiles of user groups with similar behavior and needs.
keyTerms.cx: The shareable profile is the persona; a story describes features and content intended to meet needs.

scenario.su: A team must classify materials before making a design choice while keeping that choice connected to evidence. A profile groups similar behavior and needs, while a story describes features and content and remains linked to its source need for evaluation.
scenario.ma: Compare the shareable profile’s behavior-and-needs passage, the user story’s features-and-content passage, the linkage notation connecting that story to its source need.

mc.q: A team compares a shareable user-group profile with higher-level, more stable user needs; which distinction accurately classifies the observed materials?
op: Persona stays higher-level; needs profile similar behavior
Persona describes features; needs present research findings
Persona profiles similar needs; needs describe features
Persona profiles similar behavior and needs; needs are higher-level
mc.ex: The persona profiles a group with similar behavior and needs, while user needs are higher-level and more stable than interface requests. Describing features belongs to user stories, not user needs.

mc.q: A team reviews a user story describing features and content plus a notation linking it to its source need; which classification supports evaluation?
op: Linked story enables evaluation of need fulfillment
User need enables description of story fulfillment
Story presents findings intended to meet content
Research findings enable evaluation of need fulfillment
mc.ex: The story describes features and content intended to meet a need, and its source link enables evaluation of whether that need is met. Presenting research findings is a role of personas, not the story-to-need link.

facts: Electric charge is a conserved property of matter that comes in positive and negative forms and determines electric interactions.
Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
Net charge is conserved in an isolated system.

keyTerms.df: Electric charge is a conserved property of matter that determines electric interactions.
keyTerms.eg: Matter has electric charge in positive and negative forms.
keyTerms.mi: Electric charge comes in a positive form and determines no electric interactions.
keyTerms.cx: The property includes negative as well as positive forms and determines electric interactions.

keyTerms.df: Like charges are charges distinguished by their repelling electric interaction.
keyTerms.eg: Like charges repel during electric interactions.
keyTerms.mi: Like charges attract during electric interactions.
keyTerms.cx: Repulsion, rather than attraction, describes the interaction between like charges.

keyTerms.df: An isolated system is the stated setting in which conservation applies to net charge.
keyTerms.eg: Matter with positive and negative forms is recorded in an isolated system.
keyTerms.mi: Within an isolated system, net charge is not conserved.
keyTerms.cx: The system designation requires treating its net charge as conserved.

scenario.su: Students must classify a charge record using positive-form and negative-form notations alongside like-charge and unlike-charge observations. They must choose one label before a deadline, although the interaction passage and conservation passage appear similar.
scenario.ma: positive-form notation, negative-form notation, like-charge observation, unlike-charge observation, isolated-system net-charge record

mc.q: Two observations show like charges moving apart and unlike charges moving together; which comparison correctly distinguishes the electric interactions described by those observations?
op: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
Like charges attract; unlike charges repel.
Like and unlike charges both repel.
Like and unlike charges both attract.
mc.ex: Like charges repel, whereas unlike charges attract. The reversed comparison incorrectly assigns attraction to like charges and repulsion to unlike charges.

mc.q: An isolated-system record displays net charge at the beginning and end; which label should students apply when the decision must follow the stated conservation relation?
op: Net charge is conserved in isolated system.
Net charge is not conserved in isolated system.
Net charge determines electric interactions in matter.
Electric charge comes in positive form.
mc.ex: Net charge is conserved in an isolated system. Describing it as not conserved reverses the stated relation for that setting.

facts: A service blueprint maps how a service works across user actions, visible interactions, backstage activities, and supporting operations.
A service blueprint clarifies relationships among systems and processes and can expose improvement opportunities.
Unlike a journey map, a service blueprint includes operational layers beyond the user perspective.
The diagram separates user steps, frontstage actions, backstage actions, and support processes.
Blueprint evidence can come from desk research and interviews with users, staff, and stakeholders.

keyTerms.df: A service blueprint is a diagram that includes the user perspective and operational layers beyond that perspective.
keyTerms.eg: A service blueprint maps user actions, visible interactions, backstage activities, and supporting operations.
keyTerms.mi: A service blueprint covers the user perspective while a journey map includes the operational layers.
keyTerms.cx: The operational layers belong to the service blueprint, which extends beyond the perspective represented by the journey map.

keyTerms.df: A journey map represents the user perspective, whereas a service blueprint includes operational layers beyond it.
keyTerms.eg: A comparison places the journey map at the user perspective and the service blueprint across operational layers.
keyTerms.mi: A journey map separates backstage actions and support processes as operational layers.
keyTerms.cx: Those operational layers are included in the service blueprint rather than the journey map.

keyTerms.df: Backstage actions are a distinct part of the diagram, separated from user steps, frontstage actions, and support processes.
keyTerms.eg: The diagram places backstage actions apart from frontstage actions and support processes.
keyTerms.mi: Backstage actions and frontstage actions occupy the same diagram section.
keyTerms.cx: The diagram separates backstage actions from frontstage actions.

scenario.su: Staff must classify a diagram as a service blueprint or journey map before an interview with stakeholders. The diagram separates user steps, frontstage actions, backstage actions, and support processes, while its notes show relationships among systems and processes.
scenario.ma: Compare the diagram’s four labeled sections, the notes showing relationships among systems and processes, the interview record from staff and stakeholders.

mc.q: When comparing a service blueprint with a journey map, the observed diagram extends past the user perspective into operational layers; which proposition matches that distinction?
op: Journey map includes operational layers beyond user perspective
Journey map contains the service blueprint distinction
Service blueprint includes operational layers beyond user perspective
Operational layers include a journey map
mc.ex: A service blueprint includes operational layers beyond the user perspective. Assigning those layers to the journey map reverses the stated distinction.

mc.q: Staff observe separated user steps, frontstage actions, backstage actions, and support processes before a stakeholder interview; how should they classify the diagram under the time constraint?
op: Service blueprint with separated operational layers
Journey map with separated operational layers
Operational layers containing a service blueprint
Service blueprint merging the listed operational layers
mc.ex: The separated sections are blueprint operational layers extending beyond the user perspective. Calling the diagram a journey map transfers the blueprint’s distinguishing property to the contrasting map.

facts: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a simpler version of the same problem; a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case.
A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input.
The process continues until the problem is small enough that the solution is known or easily found — the base case.
Without a base case that stops the self-calls, recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack.

keyTerms.df: Recursion reduces a problem to a simpler version of the same problem.
keyTerms.eg: Recursion continues through smaller inputs until reaching a base case.
keyTerms.mi: Recursion reaches the base case before reducing the problem.
keyTerms.cx: The problem is reduced through self-calls before the process reaches the base case.

keyTerms.df: A recursive function is distinguished by calling itself on a smaller input.
keyTerms.eg: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until reaching a base case.
keyTerms.mi: A recursive function reaches a base case before calling itself.
keyTerms.cx: Its self-calls continue on smaller inputs until the base case is reached.

keyTerms.df: A base case is the point where the solution is known or easily found.
keyTerms.eg: The process reaches a base case when the problem is small enough.
keyTerms.mi: A base case continues the self-calls on smaller inputs.
keyTerms.cx: The base case stops the self-calls instead of continuing them.

scenario.su: A reviewer must classify two recursive-function designs before a decision deadline. Both show self-calls on smaller inputs, but one reaches a base case while the other continues without a base case.
scenario.ma: Design A notation: self-calls on smaller inputs until a base case, Design B notation: self-calls on smaller inputs without a base case

mc.q: A passage compares a self-call on a smaller input with a base case that stops self-calls; which option preserves the distinct role of each exact term?
op: Self-call uses smaller input; base case stops process
Self-call uses base case; smaller input stops process
Base case uses smaller input; self-call stops process
Base case self-calls on a smaller input

facts: Electric charge is a conserved property of matter that comes in positive and negative forms and determines electric interactions.

Net charge is conserved in an isolated system.

keyTerms.eg: Positive and negative forms are forms of electric charge.
keyTerms.mi: Electric charge is a property of matter that is not conserved.
keyTerms.cx: Conservation applies to electric charge as a property of matter.

keyTerms.df: Like charges are charges whose stated electric interaction is repulsion.
keyTerms.eg: Like charges repel, while unlike charges attract.
keyTerms.mi: Like charges attract while unlike charges repel.
keyTerms.cx: Repulsion belongs to like charges, and attraction belongs to unlike charges.

keyTerms.df: Net charge is charge distinguished by conservation in an isolated system.

keyTerms.mi: Net charge is conserved in positive and negative forms.
keyTerms.cx: Positive and negative are forms of electric charge; the isolated-system relation concerns net-charge conservation.

scenario.ma: the positive-and-negative-forms passage, the like-charges-repel observation, the unlike-charges-attract observation, the isolated-system net-charge notation

Electric charge determines interactions; unlike charges repel

facts: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers.
At the equilibrium price the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and the price has no tendency to change.
A price above equilibrium creates a surplus that pushes it down; a price below creates a shortage that pushes it up.

keyTerms.df: The equilibrium price is the market price where buyer and seller quantities are equal.
keyTerms.eg: At the equilibrium price, opposing demand and supply pressures are balanced.
keyTerms.mi: The equilibrium price is the price above equilibrium that creates a surplus.
keyTerms.cx: A surplus corresponds to a price above equilibrium, not to equilibrium itself.

keyTerms.df: A surplus is the condition created when a price is above equilibrium.
keyTerms.eg: A surplus pushes the price down toward equilibrium.
keyTerms.mi: A surplus is created when the price is below equilibrium.
keyTerms.cx: Below-equilibrium pricing produces a shortage; surplus corresponds to above-equilibrium pricing.

keyTerms.df: A shortage is the condition created when a price is below equilibrium.
keyTerms.eg: A shortage pushes the price up toward equilibrium.
keyTerms.mi: A shortage is created when the price is above equilibrium.
keyTerms.cx: Above-equilibrium pricing produces a surplus; shortage corresponds to below-equilibrium pricing.

scenario.su: Buyers and sellers report quantities at a recorded price, and the quantities are equal while demand and supply pressures are balanced. A reviewer must classify the market condition before a deadline, but the label must fit the quantity comparison and pressure observation.
scenario.ma: quantity demanded by buyers record, quantity supplied by sellers record, demand and supply pressure observation

mc.q: A record shows equal quantities demanded and supplied, while a comparison shows balanced demand and supply pressures; what distinction connects market equilibrium with the equilibrium price?
op: Unequal quantities mark equilibrium; balanced pressures stabilize price
Balanced pressures mark equilibrium; equal quantities change price
Equal quantities mark equilibrium; balanced pressures change price
Equal quantities mark equilibrium; balanced pressures stabilize price
mc.ex: Equal buyer and seller quantities mark market equilibrium, while balanced demand and supply pressures mean the price has no tendency to change. Balanced pressures do not make the price tend to change.

mc.q: A reviewer observes a price above equilibrium and must classify the resulting condition and direction of pressure before a deadline; which conclusion fits the observation?
op: Classify a shortage pushing price up
Classify a shortage pushing price down
Classify a surplus pushing price down
Classify a surplus pushing price up
mc.ex: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus that pushes the price down. A shortage pushing price up corresponds to a price below equilibrium.

facts: An electric field describes the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.
The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
Field-line density indicates relative field strength.

keyTerms.df: An electric field is a description of electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.
keyTerms.eg: At each point in space, electric force per unit positive test charge specifies the electric field.
keyTerms.mi: The electric field points opposite the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
keyTerms.cx: Its direction agrees with the positive test charge's acceleration direction, rather than opposing it.

keyTerms.df: A positive test charge is the charge for which electric force per unit charge describes the electric field.
keyTerms.eg: The charge's acceleration direction identifies the direction of the electric field at a point in space.
keyTerms.mi: Field-line density gives the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
keyTerms.cx: Acceleration direction establishes field direction; density instead indicates relative field strength.

keyTerms.df: Field-line density is the field-line property that indicates relative field strength.
keyTerms.eg: Comparing density at two points in space provides a comparison of relative field strength.
keyTerms.mi: Relative field strength indicates field-line density.
keyTerms.cx: The stated relation runs from the density of field lines to comparative strength, not in reverse.

scenario.su: A student must label two electric-field descriptions before a deadline, using a direction record and a field-line-density comparison. One description records where a positive test charge would accelerate, while the other compares denser and less dense field lines, so each label must follow the relevant relation.
scenario.ma: positive-test-charge acceleration direction record, denser-versus-less-dense field-line comparison, electric-force-per-unit-positive-test-charge passage

mc.q: At one point in space, a record gives electric force per unit positive test charge and an arrow gives the positive test charge's acceleration direction; what distinction is supported?
op: Field describes force per charge; direction follows acceleration
Field describes acceleration; direction follows force per charge
Direction describes force per charge; field follows acceleration
Field describes force per charge; direction omitted
mc.ex: The electric field describes electric force per unit positive test charge, while its direction follows the positive test charge's acceleration direction. Swapping those relations incorrectly makes acceleration describe the field itself.

mc.q: Two field-line displays differ in density, with the first visibly denser than the second; under a deadline, which comparison should the student record from that observation?
op: First has greater relative field strength
Second has greater relative field strength
First has the positive charge direction
Second describes force per positive charge
mc.ex: Field-line density indicates relative field strength, so the denser first display supports greater relative strength. Assigning greater strength to the less dense second display reverses the supplied relation.

facts: People who have given up looking for work are classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed.
Discouraged workers who are excluded make unemployment look lower than the felt experience of joblessness.
Where this boundary is drawn changes the measured unemployment rate.

keyTerms.df: The labor force is a classification category that excludes people who have given up looking for work.
keyTerms.eg: People who have given up looking for work are placed out of the labor force.
keyTerms.mi: Giving up looking for work places people among the unemployed.
keyTerms.cx: Those people belong outside the labor force classification rather than among the unemployed.

keyTerms.df: Discouraged workers are excluded workers whose exclusion makes unemployment look lower than felt joblessness.
keyTerms.eg: Excluded discouraged workers make unemployment look lower than the felt experience of joblessness.
keyTerms.mi: Excluding discouraged workers makes unemployment look higher than felt joblessness.
keyTerms.cx: Their exclusion lowers how unemployment looks relative to the experience of joblessness.

keyTerms.df: The unemployment rate is a measured rate that changes according to where the classification boundary is drawn.
keyTerms.eg: Drawing the boundary differently changes the measured unemployment rate.
keyTerms.mi: The measured unemployment rate determines where the boundary is drawn.
keyTerms.cx: Boundary placement affects the measured rate, rather than the measured rate setting the boundary.

scenario.su: An analyst must classify people whose record says they have given up looking for work before approving a measured unemployment rate. A draft labels them unemployed, but the classification record places them out of the labor force, creating a boundary dispute that must be resolved.
scenario.ma: classification record stating that people have given up looking for work, draft unemployment-rate notation labeling them unemployed, boundary notation excluding discouraged workers

mc.q: A classification record identifies people who have given up looking for work, while a draft labels them unemployed. Which distinction matches the labor force boundary?
op: Out of the labor force, not unemployed
Out of the labor force and unemployed
Unemployed, not out of the labor force
Discouraged workers make unemployment look lower
mc.ex: People who have given up looking for work are classified as out of the labor force and not unemployed. Labeling them unemployed reverses the supplied classification.

mc.q: An analyst compares a classification record with an unemployment-rate notation and finds the boundary for excluded discouraged workers drawn differently. What conclusion follows from that comparison?
op: Excluded workers make unemployment look higher
Measured unemployment rate changes boundary placement
Boundary placement changes the measured unemployment rate
Boundary placement changes felt joblessness
mc.ex: The measured unemployment rate changes when the boundary is drawn differently. The rate does not determine where the boundary is placed.

facts: The four broad tissue categories are epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissue, each with structures and functions that support body organization.
Histology studies tissue appearance, organization, and function under the microscope.
Tissue cells share morphological features and an orderly arrangement that supports tissue function.

keyTerms.df: Tissue categories are broad groupings distinguished by structures and functions that support body organization.
keyTerms.eg: Epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissue are tissue categories.
keyTerms.mi: Tissue categories describe the appearance studied under the microscope.
keyTerms.cx: Appearance under the microscope belongs to what histology studies, rather than what defines the four broad groupings.

keyTerms.df: Histology is the study of tissue appearance, organization, and function under the microscope.
keyTerms.eg: Histology compares tissue appearance with tissue organization under the microscope.
keyTerms.mi: Histology is one of the four broad tissue categories.
keyTerms.cx: The four broad groupings are epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissue; histology studies tissues.

keyTerms.df: Morphological features are shared features of tissue cells associated with their orderly arrangement and tissue function.
keyTerms.eg: Tissue cells can share morphological features within an orderly arrangement.
keyTerms.mi: Morphological features are the four broad categories of tissue.
keyTerms.cx: Epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous name the categories, whereas morphological features are shared by tissue cells.

scenario.su: A student must label a comparison as tissue-category evidence or histology evidence before a deadline. scenario.ma: category list notation, microscope appearance observations, tissue organization observations

mc.q: A comparison names epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissue, while a microscope record describes tissue appearance and organization. Which distinction matches these concrete observations?
op: Categories group tissues; histology studies microscope features
Histology groups tissues; categories study microscope features
Histology omits function; categories omit organization
Categories study appearance; histology lists four tissues
mc.ex: The four names are broad tissue categories, while histology studies tissue appearance, organization, and function under the microscope. Histology does not group the four tissues; it studies tissues microscopically.

mc.q: Under a deadline, a student sees shared morphological features and an orderly arrangement in tissue cells. Which notation is supported by those observations?
op: Tissue function supports shared cell features
Cell appearance and function define histology
Cell features and arrangement support tissue function
Orderly arrangement names four tissue categories
mc.ex: Shared morphological features and an orderly arrangement of tissue cells support tissue function. The supplied relation runs from those cellular properties to tissue function, not from function to shared features.

facts: The rock cycle describes the continuing transformation of crustal materials and is driven by Earth's internal heat engine and the solar-powered hydrological cycle.

keyTerms.mi: The rock cycle describes the movement of water, ice, and air at the surface.
keyTerms.cx: Movement of water, ice, and air at the surface belongs to the hydrological cycle, while the rock cycle concerns crustal materials.

keyTerms.mi: Earth's internal heat moves water, ice, and air at the surface.
keyTerms.cx: Water, ice, and air are moved at the surface by the hydrological cycle, not by Earth's internal heat.

keyTerms.cx: Movement through the core and mantle is associated with Earth's internal heat, whereas the hydrological cycle operates at the surface.

facts: Capacitance is the ratio of stored charge to potential difference for a conductor or capacitor.

keyTerms.mi: Capacitance is the energy stored between a capacitor's conductors.
keyTerms.cx: Energy is stored in the electric field; the charge-to-potential-difference relation identifies capacitance.

keyTerms.mi: The electric field is the ratio of stored charge to potential difference.
keyTerms.cx: That ratio describes capacitance, whereas stored energy is associated with the field between conductors.

keyTerms.cx: For parallel plates, a rise in area goes with a rise, rather than a fall, in capacitance.

facts: Functional harmony classifies chords by the role they play in a progression, especially tonic, dominant, and pre-dominant functions.
The tonic is built on scale degree one, while pre-dominants are built on degrees two, three, four, and six.
In minor, raising the third of the fifth-degree chord makes it major and strengthens its dominant function.

keyTerms.df: Functional harmony is a classification of chords according to their roles in a progression.
keyTerms.eg: A progression classified with tonic, dominant, and pre-dominant functions uses functional harmony.
keyTerms.mi: Functional harmony classifies chords by scale degree rather than their role in a progression.
keyTerms.cx: The classification depends on each chord's role in the progression, not a replacement of role by scale degree.

keyTerms.df: The tonic is a chord function distinguished by being built on scale degree one.
keyTerms.eg: In a progression, the scale-degree-one chord receives the tonic label.
keyTerms.mi: A chord built on scale degree four has tonic function.
keyTerms.cx: Degree four supports a pre-dominant classification, while degree one supports the tonic classification.

keyTerms.df: Dominant function is the role strengthened when a minor fifth-degree chord has its third raised.
keyTerms.eg: In minor, the raised-third fifth-degree chord becomes major.
keyTerms.mi: Raising the third of the fifth-degree chord weakens its dominant function.
keyTerms.cx: The raised third strengthens the chord's dominant role instead of weakening it.

scenario.su: A student editor must classify two chord notations before a deadline: one is built on scale degree one, and one is built on scale degree four. The editor must choose tonic or pre-dominant for each notation and justify both labels from the recorded scale degrees.

mc.q: An editor observes one chord built on scale degree one and another on degree four; which comparison correctly distinguishes their tonic and pre-dominant functions?
op: Degree one is tonic; degree four is pre-dominant
Degree four is tonic; degree one is pre-dominant
Degrees one and four are pre-dominant functions
Degrees one and four are tonic functions
mc.ex: The tonic is built on degree one, while degree four is among the degrees supporting pre-dominants. Assigning tonic to degree four and pre-dominant to degree one reverses these supplied relationships.

mc.q: In minor, an analyst observes that the third of a fifth-degree chord was raised and must classify the resulting chord and function before a deadline; which decision fits?
op: Classify it as major with strengthened dominant function
Classify it as minor with strengthened dominant function
Classify it as major with strengthened tonic function
Classify it as major with strengthened pre-dominant function
mc.ex: Raising the third makes the minor fifth-degree chord major and strengthens its dominant function. Retaining a minor classification contradicts the stated change produced by raising the third.
